api.name: Yoruba Recipe API
api.description: A comprehensive collection of authentic Yoruba and indigenous Southwest Nigerian recipes with full nutritional data, cooking instructions, and cultural context.
api.author: Yoruba Recipe API

foods.name: Ewedu Soup
health_benefits: rich in vitamins A and C
instructions: Wash the jute leaves thoroughly and pluck leaves from the stems, discarding the stems.
Place leaves in a blender with a small amount of water and blend until smooth and slightly slimy, or use a traditional ijabe broom whisk.
Pour blended ewedu into a pot over medium heat.
Add a tiny pinch of kaun (potash) to maintain the green colour and help thicken.
Add locust beans and ground crayfish, stir well.
Cook for 5-7 minutes stirring continuously.
Season with salt to taste.
Remove from heat immediately once smooth and slightly viscous — do not overcook.
Serve hot alongside amala, eba, or pounded yam.
foods.image_credit: Bukky658, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

foods.name: Gbegiri
instructions: Soak beans for 30 minutes, then peel skins by rubbing between palms and rinsing off husks.
Boil peeled beans in a pot for 45-60 minutes until completely soft and mashable.
Drain excess water and mash or blend into a smooth paste.
In a separate pot heat palm oil over medium heat for 2 minutes.
Add chopped onions and fry until translucent, about 3 minutes.
Add blended scotch bonnet and fry for another 5 minutes until raw pepper smell disappears.
Add mashed bean paste and stir to combine with the oil and pepper base.
Add locust beans and ground crayfish, stir thoroughly.
Add a little water to achieve a thick pourable soup consistency.
Season with salt, cover and simmer on low heat for 10 minutes stirring occasionally.
Serve alongside amala and ewedu as part of the classic Yoruba trio.
foods.image_credit: Bukky658, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

foods.name: Okra Soup
instructions: Season and boil meat or fish with onions and salt until tender. Set aside the stock.
Wash fresh okra and slice into thin rounds 3-5mm thick, or blend roughly for a slimier texture.
Heat palm oil in a pot over medium heat.
Add chopped onions and sauté for 2 minutes.
Add blended scotch bonnet pepper and fry for 5 minutes stirring often.
Add the meat stock and bring to a boil.
Add the cooked meat and fish to the pot.
Add ground crayfish and locust beans and stir well.
Add the sliced okra and stir gently — do not cover the pot as this causes okra to lose its colour.
Cook on medium heat for 5-7 minutes until okra is just cooked but still bright.
Season with salt and remove from heat.
Serve with amala, eba, or pounded yam.
foods.image_credit: CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

foods.name: Egusi Soup
instructions: Season and boil meat and fish with onions and salt until tender. Reserve the stock.
Blend tomatoes, scotch bonnet pepper and half the onions into a smooth paste.
Mix ground egusi with a little water to form a thick paste to prevent lumps.
Heat palm oil in a large pot over medium heat.
Add remaining sliced onions and fry for 2 minutes.
Add the blended tomato-pepper paste and fry on medium-high heat for 15 minutes stirring often until oil floats to the top.
Push pepper mix to the sides and add egusi paste in spoonfuls into the centre of the pot.
Allow egusi to fry in the oil for 5 minutes without stirring to form a slight crust, then stir everything together.
Add meat stock gradually, stir and bring to a simmer.
Add cooked meat, fish, locust beans and crayfish. Cook for 10 minutes.
Wash and roughly chop leafy greens then add to the pot.
Season with salt, stir and cook for a final 3-5 minutes. Do not overcook the greens.
Serve hot with amala, pounded yam or eba.
foods.image_credit: CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

foods.name: Ogbono Soup
instructions: Season and cook meat and fish until tender. Keep the stock.
Blend scotch bonnet pepper and onions together and set aside.
Heat palm oil in a pot over medium heat.
Add ground ogbono directly into the hot oil and stir quickly and continuously — ogbono draws almost immediately.
Stir for 3-4 minutes until ogbono is dissolved into the oil and smells nutty.
Add blended pepper and stir to combine.
Add reserved meat stock gradually, stirring to prevent lumps. The soup will become thick and draw.
Add cooked meat and fish, locust beans and crayfish.
Cover and simmer on low heat for 15 minutes, stirring every few minutes.
Add chopped leafy vegetables, stir and cook uncovered for a further 3-5 minutes.
Season with salt to taste and serve with pounded yam, amala or eba.

foods.name: Goat Meat Pepper Soup

ingredients.name: pepper soup spice mix
ingredients.substitution: mix of uziza, ehuru, uda and crayfish

instructions: Wash the goat meat thoroughly, scrubbing with salt and rinsing under cold water.
Place meat in a pot with onions, half the scotch bonnet, salt and a little water.
Parboil for 10 minutes on high heat to remove impurities, then drain and discard the parboiling water.
Return meat to the pot, add fresh water to cover and boil on medium heat for 30-40 minutes until tender.
Add the pepper soup spice mix, remaining scotch bonnet and ground crayfish.
Stir well and taste — adjust salt and spice to preference.
Reduce heat to low and simmer for another 10 minutes to allow spices to infuse fully.
Add fresh scent leaves in the last 2 minutes — do not overcook the leaves.
Serve hot as a standalone soup or with a small portion of eba or boiled yam.
foods.image_credit: CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

foods.name: Ayamase
instructions: Season and cook assorted meats with onions and salt until very tender. Reserve the meat stock.
Blend green bell peppers and scotch bonnet coarsely — not too smooth.
To bleach the palm oil: heat in a dry pot on high heat with the lid on for 10-15 minutes until it turns clear and golden and the smoke dies down.
Allow bleached oil to cool slightly then carefully add the blended green pepper mixture.
Fry the pepper in the bleached oil over medium heat, stirring frequently for 20-25 minutes until water evaporates and oil rises to the top.
Add locust beans and crayfish, stir well.
Add the cooked assorted meats and the reserved meat stock.
Stir and cook on medium heat for another 10 minutes.
Add hard boiled eggs whole or halved in the last 5 minutes.
Season with salt to taste and serve over ofada rice.
foods.image_credit: Placeholder — replace with actual food photograph

foods.name: Obe Ata
health_benefits: rich in antioxidants from peppers and tomatoes
instructions: Season and boil meat and fish with onions and salt until tender. Reserve the stock.
Blend tomatoes, red bell peppers, scotch bonnet and half the onions into a smooth paste.
Heat palm oil in a pot over medium heat.
Add remaining sliced onions and fry until golden, about 3 minutes.
Add blended pepper-tomato mixture and fry on medium-high heat for 20 minutes stirring regularly until sauce is thick and oil floats on top.
Add locust beans and crayfish and stir.
Add cooked meats and fish with a little reserved stock.
Cover and simmer on low heat for 10 minutes.
Season with salt to taste.
Serve with boiled yam, roasted yam, eba, amala or white rice.
foods.image_credit: Placeholder — replace with actual food photograph

foods.name: Fresh Fish Soup

ingredients.name: fresh whole fish tilapia or catfish

instructions: Clean fresh fish thoroughly — remove scales, guts and gills. Score the flesh with diagonal cuts.
Season fish with salt and a little pepper and set aside for 10 minutes.
Blend scotch bonnet and half the onions into a rough paste.
Heat palm oil in a wide pot over medium heat.
Add remaining sliced onions and fry gently for 2 minutes.
Add blended pepper and fry for 5 minutes until slightly reduced.
Add about 300ml of water and bring to a boil.
Add ground crayfish and locust beans and stir.
Gently lower the seasoned fish into the pot — handle carefully so it does not break apart.
Cook on medium heat for 12-15 minutes until fish is fully cooked through.
Add fresh scent leaves in the final minute.
Season with salt, adjust taste and serve hot with amala, eba or boiled yam.
foods.image_credit: Placeholder — replace with actual food photograph

foods.name: Smoked Fish Soup
instructions: Soak smoked fish in hot water for 5-10 minutes to soften, then debone carefully and flake into chunks.
Blend tomatoes, scotch bonnet and onions into a smooth paste.
Heat palm oil in a pot over medium heat.
Add sliced onions and fry gently for 2 minutes.
Add blended tomato-pepper paste and fry for 10-12 minutes stirring until oil rises to the top.
Add locust beans and ground crayfish and stir well.
Add about 200ml of water and bring to a simmer.
Add the flaked smoked fish gently.
Cook for 8-10 minutes on low heat to allow fish flavour to fully infuse the soup.
Season with salt — remember smoked fish is already salty so taste before adding.
Serve with amala, eba or boiled yam.
foods.image_credit: Placeholder — replace with actual food photograph

foods.name: Efo Riro
health_benefits: very rich in iron and vitamins from leafy greens

ingredients.name: shredded African spinach or water leaf

instructions: Season and cook assorted meat and fish until tender. Reserve the stock.
Wash leafy greens thoroughly, shred finely and squeeze out excess water. Set aside.
Blend red bell pepper, scotch bonnet and half the onions together.
Heat palm oil in a wide pot over medium-high heat.
Add remaining sliced onions and fry for 2 minutes.
Add blended pepper mixture and fry for 15 minutes stirring often until oil rises to the surface.
Add locust beans and crayfish and stir well.
Add cooked meats and fish with a splash of meat stock. Cook for 5 minutes.
Add shredded leafy greens and stir to combine with the sauce.
Do not cover the pot — cook on medium heat for 5-7 minutes stirring occasionally.
Greens should be wilted but still vibrant in colour — do not overcook.
Season with salt and serve with amala, eba or pounded yam.
foods.image_credit: Placeholder — replace with actual food photograph

foods.name: Fried Pepper Stew
instructions: Season and cook assorted meats until tender. Reserve the stock.
Blend peppers and half the onions coarsely — the stew is better with some texture.
Heat palm oil in a pot over high heat.
Add remaining sliced onions and fry until golden brown.
Add blended pepper and fry on high heat stirring constantly for 25-30 minutes.
This long frying is the key to obe ata din din — peppers must be very well fried until almost dry and oil has fully separated.
Add locust beans and crayfish and stir.
Add cooked meats and a splash of stock.
Reduce heat to medium and cook for another 10 minutes.
Season with salt to taste.
This stew keeps well in the fridge and tastes better the next day. Serve with rice, yam or as a base for other soups.
foods.image_credit: Placeholder — replace with actual food photograph

foods.name: Isapa Soup
health_benefits: unique sour flavour from roselle leaves
instructions: If using dried isapa, soak in water for 10 minutes to rehydrate. If fresh, wash thoroughly.
Soak and debone smoked fish then flake into pieces.
Blend or roughly chop scotch bonnet and onions.
Heat palm oil in a pot over medium heat.
Add onions and fry gently for 2 minutes.
Add blended pepper and fry for 5 minutes.
Add isapa leaves directly to the pot — they will release a sour liquid as they cook.
Add about 200ml of water and stir to combine.
Add smoked fish, locust beans and crayfish.
Cook on medium-low heat for 15 minutes — the sourness of isapa mellows as it cooks.
Season with salt to taste.
Serve alongside amala or pounded yam.
foods.image_credit: Placeholder — replace with actual food photograph

foods.name: Cocoyam Pepper Soup
instructions: Peel and cut cocoyam into bite-sized chunks, rinse and set aside.
Soak and debone smoked fish, flake into pieces.
Blend scotch bonnet and onions together.
Place cocoyam in a pot, cover with water and boil for 20 minutes until soft but not falling apart.
Drain most of the water leaving just enough to cover the cocoyam.
Add palm oil, blended pepper, locust beans and crayfish.
Add the flaked smoked fish.
Stir gently and cook on medium heat for 15 minutes — cocoyam will slightly thicken the soup naturally.
Season with salt to taste.
Serve as a standalone soup or alongside amala.
foods.image_credit: Placeholder — replace with actual food photograph

foods.name: Amala
instructions: Bring water to a full rolling boil in a medium pot over high heat.
Gradually sprinkle yam flour into the boiling water in small amounts, stirring vigorously with a wooden spatula between each addition to prevent lumps.
Once all flour is added and mixture is thick, reduce heat to low.
Cover the pot and allow to steam for 3-5 minutes.
Stir again vigorously, folding from the bottom up until very smooth and uniform — amala should be dark brown and stretchy.
If too stiff, add a small splash of hot water and stir again.
Mould into smooth balls using a wet bowl and a spatula, or serve directly.
Serve immediately alongside ewedu, gbegiri, okra soup or egusi.
foods.image_credit: Bukky658, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

foods.name: Eba
instructions: Bring water to a full boil.
Pour boiling water into a bowl or pot.
Gradually pour in garri while stirring continuously with a wooden spatula.
Keep stirring and adding garri in small amounts until mixture becomes firm and pulls away from the sides.
Eba should be stiff enough to hold its shape but not dry or crumbly.
Cover with a lid for 2 minutes to allow it to steam and become smooth.
Stir once more then mould into a ball using a wet bowl.
Serve hot with any Yoruba soup — efo riro, egusi, okra or ogbono.
foods.image_credit: CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

foods.name: Pounded Yam
instructions: Peel the yam and cut into chunks. Remove any brown or discoloured spots.
Wash yam chunks thoroughly under running water.
Place in a pot, cover with water and boil over medium-high heat for 20-25 minutes until completely soft.
Drain all water completely — excess water makes pounded yam sticky rather than stretchy.
Transfer hot yam into a mortar and begin pounding with a pestle.
Pound continuously folding the yam over itself between strokes.
Add a tablespoon of hot water if the mixture becomes too stiff while pounding.
Continue pounding for 10-15 minutes until completely smooth, stretchy and lump-free.
To test: pull a small piece — it should stretch without breaking and have no lumps.
Mould into smooth balls and serve immediately with any Yoruba soup.
foods.image_credit: Placeholder — replace with actual food photograph

foods.name: Plantain Flour Swallow
instructions: Bring water to a rolling boil.
Reduce heat to medium and gradually sprinkle plantain flour into the boiling water while stirring constantly.
Stir vigorously to prevent lumps — plantain flour is slightly denser than yam flour.
Once all flour is incorporated, cover the pot and steam on low heat for 5 minutes.
Stir again thoroughly — amala ogede will be greyish-brown in colour with an earthy plantain scent.
If too stiff add a little hot water and fold in.
Mould and serve alongside gbegiri, ewedu or efo riro.
foods.image_credit: Placeholder — replace with actual food photograph

foods.name: Lafun
instructions: Bring water to a full boil in a pot.
Reduce to medium heat and gradually add lafun flour stirring constantly as you pour.
Lafun has a slightly sour fermented aroma — this is normal and part of its character.
Stir vigorously to remove all lumps. The mixture will be white and thicker than eba.
Cover and steam on low heat for 5 minutes.
Stir again to check smoothness. Lafun should be smooth and slightly stretchy but softer than amala.
Add a tiny splash of hot water if needed to loosen.
Mould and serve with ewedu, egusi or efo riro.
foods.image_credit: Placeholder — replace with actual food photograph

foods.name: Pounded Cocoyam
instructions: Peel cocoyam carefully — the skin can cause itching, so wear gloves or peel under running water.
Cut into chunks and boil in water for 25-30 minutes until very soft.
Drain all water completely.
Transfer hot cocoyam to a mortar and pound.
Cocoyam is more slippery than yam when pounding — use firm rhythmic strokes.
The cocoyam will become very smooth and slightly sticky — this is the desired texture.
Do not add water unless absolutely necessary as cocoyam naturally has more moisture than yam.
Mould and serve with okra soup, efo riro or egusi.
foods.image_credit: Placeholder — replace with actual food photograph

foods.name: Ofada Rice
instructions: Wash ofada rice thoroughly multiple times — it has a natural earthy aroma which is part of its character.
Optional: parboil and rinse once to reduce the strong aroma — soak in hot water for 10 minutes, drain and proceed.
Place washed rice in a pot, cover with fresh water at 2.5x the volume of rice and bring to a boil.
Add a pinch of salt, reduce heat to low and cover tightly.
Cook for 35-40 minutes until all water is absorbed and rice is cooked through — ofada takes longer than regular rice.
Do not lift the lid too often — the steam is essential for even cooking.
Fluff with a fork and serve with ayamase or obe ata.
foods.image_credit: Placeholder — replace with actual food photograph

foods.name: Boiled Yam
instructions: Peel the yam and cut into round slices about 2cm thick.
Wash the yam pieces under running water.
Place in a pot and cover with cold water. Add a pinch of salt.
Bring to a boil over high heat then reduce to medium.
Cook for 20-25 minutes until tender — a fork should pass through cleanly with no resistance.
Drain water and serve hot with egg sauce, obe ata or palm oil.
foods.image_credit: CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

foods.name: Roasted Yam
instructions: Wash the unpeeled yam and slice into rounds about 2-3cm thick — the skin protects the yam during roasting.
Place slices directly on an open charcoal grill or under a broiler preheated to 220°C.
Roast for 12-15 minutes per side turning once until skin is charred and inside is fully cooked through.
To test doneness press the yam — it should feel soft inside.
Peel off the charred skin and serve hot.
Traditionally served with obe ata or palm oil with garden egg.
foods.image_credit: Placeholder — replace with actual food photograph

foods.name: Roasted Plantain
instructions: Do not peel the plantain — roast it whole in the skin.
Place the whole plantain directly on a charcoal grill or under an oven broiler at 220°C.
Grill for 8-10 minutes per side turning once or twice until skin is completely charred and blackened.
The inside will be soft and sweet from natural sugars caramelising.
Remove from heat, allow to cool for 2 minutes then peel off the charred skin.
Slice and serve hot alongside groundnut or obe ata.
foods.image_credit: Placeholder — replace with actual food photograph

foods.name: Pap
instructions: Mix wet fermented maize paste with a little cold water until smooth and lump-free — about 100ml water per 200g paste.
Bring remaining water to a boil in a pot.
Gradually pour maize paste mixture into boiling water while stirring continuously in one direction.
Stir vigorously to prevent lumps — the mixture will thicken quickly.
Cook on medium heat for 5-7 minutes stirring constantly until smooth, thick and pourable.
Add sugar, honey or evaporated milk to taste if desired.
Serve hot in a bowl alongside akara, moi moi or fried fish.
foods.image_credit: Placeholder — replace with actual food photograph

foods.name: Akara
instructions: Soak beans in water for 20-30 minutes to loosen the skins.
Peel beans by rubbing vigorously between palms and rinsing repeatedly until skins are removed and beans are clean and white.
Blend peeled beans with onions and scotch bonnet pepper — add as little water as possible. Batter should be thick.
Transfer to a bowl and beat batter vigorously with a wooden spoon for 5 minutes — this introduces air and makes akara fluffy.
Season with salt and mix again.
Heat vegetable oil in a deep pot to 175°C — deep enough to submerge the akara.
Test oil with a small drop of batter — it should sizzle and float immediately.
Using a spoon scoop balls of batter and gently drop into the oil.
Fry in batches for 4-5 minutes turning once or twice until golden brown on all sides.
Remove with a slotted spoon and drain on paper towels.
Serve hot alongside pap or as a standalone breakfast snack.
foods.image_credit: CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

foods.name: Moi Moi
instructions: Soak beans for 20-30 minutes then peel by rubbing off skins and rinsing until clean.
Blend peeled beans with red bell pepper, scotch bonnet and onions. Add water gradually for a smooth but not watery batter.
Pour batter into a bowl. Add palm oil, crayfish and salt. Stir to combine.
If using eggs crack them in and stir well.
Pour batter into greased foil cups, banana leaves or a heatproof dish — fill each three-quarters full.
Place filled cups in a pot with a small amount of boiling water at the base — water should not touch the moi moi.
Cover the pot tightly and steam on medium heat for 40-45 minutes.
Replenish water at the base if it evaporates.
Moi moi is ready when firm and a skewer inserted comes out clean.
Allow to cool for 5 minutes before unwrapping. Serve as a side with pap, rice or alone.
foods.image_credit: Placeholder — replace with actual food photograph

foods.name: Adalu
health_benefits: high fiber from beans and corn
instructions: If using dry corn soak overnight or for at least 4 hours to soften.
Soak beans separately for 1 hour.
Cook corn in a pot of water for 30 minutes until partially tender.
Add soaked beans to the pot of partially cooked corn.
Continue cooking together for another 30-40 minutes until both corn and beans are completely soft.
Drain any excess water.
Add palm oil and salt, stir to coat everything.
Cook on low heat for a further 5 minutes.
Serve warm as a standalone meal or alongside fried plantain.
foods.image_credit: Placeholder — replace with actual food photograph

foods.name: Yam Porridge
instructions: Peel and cut yam into medium cubes. Wash thoroughly.
Soak and debone smoked fish then flake into pieces.
Blend scotch bonnet and onions roughly.
Place yam in a pot, add just enough water to barely cover.
Add palm oil, blended pepper, locust beans and crayfish directly to the pot with the raw yam.
Bring to a boil then reduce to medium heat.
Cook for 20-25 minutes stirring occasionally — yam will begin to break down and thicken the liquid.
Add smoked fish and stir gently.
Use a wooden spoon to partially mash some yam pieces for a creamy consistency while leaving others intact for texture.
Cook for another 5-10 minutes until thick and porridge-like.
Season with salt to taste and serve hot.
foods.image_credit: CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

foods.name: Eko

ingredients.name: banana or plantain leaves for wrapping

instructions: Mix fermented corn starch paste with cold water until smooth and lump-free.
Bring mixture to the stove over medium heat stirring constantly.
Cook for 10-15 minutes stirring without stopping until mixture thickens into a very stiff smooth paste.
Eko is ready when it pulls completely from the sides of the pot.
While still hot pour into banana leaf-lined moulds or foil containers.
Allow to cool and set completely at room temperature for at least 1 hour — eko sets firm as it cools.
Once firm unwrap and slice. Serve with efo riro, obe ata or gbegiri.
foods.image_credit: CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

foods.name: Ekuru
instructions: Soak beans for 30 minutes then peel off all skins thoroughly by rubbing and rinsing repeatedly.
Blend peeled beans with minimal water into a smooth very thick paste.
Add palm oil, locust beans, blended pepper and salt to the batter and mix well.
Unlike akara do not beat air into the batter — ekuru should be dense not fluffy.
Scoop batter into banana leaf parcels or foil cups.
Arrange in a pot with water at the base and steam on medium heat for 35-40 minutes.
Ekuru is done when firm and a skewer comes out clean.
Serve with obe ata din din or obe eja gbigbe poured over the top.
foods.image_credit: Placeholder — replace with actual food photograph

foods.name: Ojojo
instructions: Peel and grate water yam finely into a bowl — water yam is naturally slimy, this is expected.
Finely chop onions and scotch bonnet pepper and add to grated yam.
Add ground crayfish and salt then mix well.
The mixture should be thick enough to hold its shape when scooped.
Heat vegetable oil in a deep pan to 170°C.
Scoop tablespoon-sized portions and gently drop into hot oil.
Fry in batches for 4-5 minutes per side turning until golden and crispy.
Remove and drain on paper towels.
Serve hot with pap or as a standalone morning snack.
foods.image_credit: Placeholder — replace with actual food photograph

foods.name: Ikokore
health_benefits: good protein from fish and meat
instructions: Season and parboil meat and fish until partially cooked. Reserve the stock.
Peel and grate water yam — it will be very slimy. Set aside.
Blend scotch bonnet and onions together.
Heat palm oil in a pot over medium heat.
Add onions and fry for 2 minutes.
Add blended pepper and fry for 5 minutes.
Add meat stock and bring to a boil.
Add meat, fish, crayfish and locust beans.
Using a spoon drop small dollops of grated water yam into the boiling stew — the yam will set into soft dumplings.
Stir gently so as not to break the yam dumplings.
Cook on medium heat for 20-25 minutes until yam dumplings are fully cooked and stew is thick.
Season with salt to taste and serve hot. Ikokore is eaten on its own — no additional swallow needed.
foods.image_credit: Placeholder — replace with actual food photograph

foods.name: Aadun
instructions: Dry-roast corn on a pan or in an oven at 180°C until golden and fragrant then grind into a coarse flour.
Heat palm oil gently in a pan until just warm — not hot.
Mix warm palm oil with roasted corn flour, ground pepper, locust beans and salt.
Mix thoroughly with hands until mixture comes together and resembles wet sand — it should hold its shape when squeezed.
Roll into small cylindrical shapes or mould with your hands.
Aadun is served at room temperature and does not need further cooking.
Store in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days.
foods.image_credit: Placeholder — replace with actual food photograph

foods.name: Honey Beans
health_benefits: naturally lower GI than regular beans
instructions: Pick through beans and remove any stones or bad beans.
Wash thoroughly and soak for 1 hour or overnight to reduce cooking time.
Cook beans in a pot of water over medium-high heat for 45-60 minutes until completely tender and soft enough to mash easily.
While beans cook blend scotch bonnet and onions together.
In a separate pan heat palm oil and fry blended pepper for 5 minutes.
Once beans are cooked drain most of the water leaving just a little.
Add fried pepper sauce to the beans and stir.
Cook together on low heat for 10 minutes.
Season with salt — honey beans naturally have a slight sweetness so taste before adding.
Serve with fried plantain, bread or boiled yam.
foods.image_credit: Placeholder — replace with actual food photograph

combinations.name: Amala Dinner
serving_tips: Start gbegiri first — the beans take about 60 minutes to soften.
Prepare ewedu last, just before serving — it loses its green colour quickly once cooked.
Mould amala immediately before serving while it is still hot and stretchy.
Serve gbegiri and ewedu poured side by side in the same bowl, not mixed.
Amala is traditionally eaten by hand — pull a small piece and dip into both soups.

steps.action: Soak and begin cooking beans for gbegiri
Fry pepper base for gbegiri and add mashed beans
Boil water and prepare amala
Blend and cook ewedu — takes only 10 minutes
Mould amala, pour gbegiri and ewedu side by side and serve immediately

combinations.name: Eba & Egusi
serving_tips: Cook egusi soup first as it requires the most time and attention.
Make eba only when egusi is fully done — eba hardens quickly if left to sit.
Serve egusi in a deep bowl with eba on the side or on a separate plate.
Eba is best eaten immediately — do not leave it uncovered or it dries out.

steps.action: Season and boil meat and fish for egusi
Fry pepper base and egusi paste
Simmer egusi with stock, meat and greens
Boil water and make eba just before serving
Serve eba moulded alongside hot egusi soup

combinations.name: Pounded Yam & Ogbono
serving_tips: Begin the ogbono soup first — it needs time to simmer and develop its draw texture.
Pound yam while ogbono is on its final simmer so both are hot at the same time.
Pounded yam must be served immediately — it becomes stiff and rubbery if it cools.
Traditionally pounded yam is placed in a bowl and ogbono poured around it, not over it.
Use a mortar and pestle for the best stretchy texture.

steps.action: Season and boil meat and fish for ogbono
Dissolve ogbono in hot palm oil and add stock
Boil yam pieces in parallel during ogbono simmer
Simmer ogbono with meat, fish and vegetables
Pound yam in mortar until smooth and stretchy
Mould pounded yam and serve with ogbono immediately

combinations.name: Ofada Rice & Ayamase
serving_tips: Start ayamase first — bleaching palm oil and long frying of peppers takes 45 minutes.
Wash and cook ofada rice while ayamase is frying.
Ofada rice has a distinct earthy aroma — this is natural and desirable.
Traditionally served wrapped in fresh banana leaves at Yoruba events.
Spoon ayamase generously over ofada rice when serving — do not mix them in the pot.
Add the boiled eggs from ayamase on top for the full presentation.

steps.action: Season and cook assorted meats for ayamase
Bleach palm oil on high heat with lid on
Wash ofada rice and begin cooking in fresh water
Fry blended green pepper in bleached oil for 25 minutes
Add meat and eggs to ayamase and finish
Fluff ofada rice and plate with ayamase spooned over

combinations.name: Pounded Yam, Ewedu & Gbegiri
serving_tips: This is the classic Yoruba celebratory trio — served at virtually every major Yoruba event.
Begin gbegiri well in advance as beans require the longest cooking time.
Pound yam last so it is piping hot at serving time.
Ewedu must be made last of all — it takes only 10 minutes and discolours if made too early.
Serve gbegiri and ewedu together in the same soup bowl, poured side by side.
Pounded yam is served separately and eaten by dipping into both soups.

steps.action: Soak and begin boiling beans for gbegiri
Finish gbegiri — fry base and combine with mashed beans
